Explanation: These four histone types form the nucleosome core; two copies of each assemble the histone octamer. H1 is a linker histone and is not part of the core.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Nucleosome core histones; Histone octamer components
Source Section: PDF p. 8 | DNA Structure > DNA Tertiary Structure > Histones
Notes: Verified standard molecular biology: H2A/H2B/H3/H4 are core histones (octamer); H1 is the linker. No outlier.

Explanation: Irinotecan and topotecan (camptothecin derivatives) inhibit topoisomerase I; etoposide and teniposide (epipodophyllotoxins) inhibit topoisomerase II. The unifying category is the topoisomerase enzyme family, spanning both isoforms.
Source Section: PDF p. 10 | DNA Replication > Enzymes
Notes: Isoform split verified: TOP1 = irinotecan/topotecan; TOP2 = etoposide/teniposide (Yakkala et al., Pharmaceuticals 2023, PMID 37895927; Thomas & Pommier, Clin Cancer Res 2019, PMID 31227499). Board caution: do not label all four as a single isoform; avoid mixing anthracyclines (also TOP2) as distractors that break family-level logic.

Explanation: Colchicine and the vinca alkaloids (vincristine, vinblastine) inhibit tubulin polymerization; paclitaxel stabilizes microtubules and blocks depolymerization. All four perturb microtubule dynamics, in opposite directions.
Source Section: PDF p. 23 | Mitosis > Pharmacology
Notes: Verified: paclitaxel = stabilizer; vinca alkaloids and colchicine = destabilizers/polymerization inhibitors (Rowinsky & Donehower, NEJM 1995; Huang et al., Oxid Med Cell Longev 2021). Keep umbrella 'dynamics' wording; do NOT title as 'polymerization inhibitors' (excludes paclitaxel). Colchicine is not used as cancer chemotherapy.

Explanation: Each disorder is caused by an unstable triplet repeat: CGG (FMR1, Fragile X), GAA (FXN, Friedreich), CAG (HTT, Huntington), CTG (DMPK, myotonic dystrophy type 1).
Source Section: PDF pp. 42-43 | Trinucleotide Repeat Expansion Diseases
Notes: Repeat assignments verified (Zhou et al., Nat Rev Neurol 2022; Fourier & Quadrio, J Neural Transm 2022; Annear et al., BMC Genomics 2026, PMID 41709137). Keep 'type 1' for myotonic dystrophy (CTG/DMPK; DM2 is CCTG). Do not add a universal-anticipation claim.

Connection Title: Orotic aciduria from UMP synthase deficiency
Explanation: Hereditary orotic aciduria (UMP synthase deficiency) causes orotic acid accumulation, megaloblastic anemia unresponsive to B12/folate, and failure to thrive. Ammonia is normal, which distinguishes it from OTC deficiency, where orotic aciduria is accompanied by hyperammonemia.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Hereditary orotic aciduria; UMP synthase deficiency findings
Source Section: PDF p. 7 | Clinical Applications of the Pyrimidine Pathway > Pathology
Notes: Normal ammonia verified as the key discriminator from OTC deficiency (elevated orotate WITH hyperammonemia) (Brosnan & Brosnan, J Nutr 2007, PMID 17513443; Ah Mew & Lichter-Konecki, Pediatr Drugs 2025; GeneReviews OTC Deficiency 2022). Normal ammonia is a lab discriminator, not a symptom.

Explanation: Defective nucleotide excision repair in xeroderma pigmentosum causes extreme photosensitivity, premalignant actinic keratoses, early cutaneous malignancies, and ocular-surface disease. Corneal involvement most often manifests as scarring, opacity, and neovascularization rather than isolated ulceration.
Source Section: PDF pp. 18-20 | Single Stranded Repair > Nucleotide Excision Repair
Notes: Correction: Tile 4 'Corneal ulcers' revised to 'Corneal scarring/opacity' to match best-documented ocular findings (corneal scarring, neovascularization, limbal stem cell deficiency, dry eye) (Brooks et al., Ophthalmology 2013, PMID 23601806; Nandyala et al., Cornea 2021, PMID 33259350; Lim et al., Ophthalmology 2017, PMID 28554534). Findings are characteristic, not universal, and subtype-dependent. Original source supports photosensitivity, premalignant lesions, skin cancer, and corneal involvement.

Explanation: In base excision repair a DNA glycosylase removes the damaged base, AP endonuclease incises the resulting abasic site, DNA polymerase beta fills the gap, and DNA ligase seals the nick (short-patch BER).
Accepted Alternate Category Names: BER machinery; Base excision repair enzymes
Source Section: PDF pp. 18-20 | Single Stranded Repair > Base Excision Repair
Notes: Step/enzyme assignments verified (Merlin et al., Cancer Med 2025; Kim et al., Sci Rep 2023; Golato et al., Sci Rep 2017). DNA ligase and glycosylases also participate in other pathways; keep pathway-level title. Board caution: avoid co-placing NER/MMR enzymes as distractors.

Explanation: ATM-related ataxia-telangiectasia presents with progressive cerebellar ataxia, oculocutaneous telangiectasias, immunodeficiency with recurrent sinopulmonary infections, and elevated serum alpha-fetoprotein.
Source Section: PDF p. 21 | Double Stranded Repair > Ataxia Telangiectasia
Notes: All four verified, including elevated AFP as the hallmark biomarker (Nakano et al., Clin Cancer Res 2024; GeneReviews Ataxia-Telangiectasia 2025; Coarelli et al., J Neurol 2023; MedlinePlus). Telangiectasias may appear years after ataxia onset; AFP is unreliable under age 2.

Explanation: Fanconi anemia (defective interstrand-crosslink repair) is associated with progressive bone marrow failure, congenital skeletal anomalies (e.g., radial/thumb), cafe-au-lait macules, and increased risk of AML/MDS. These are associations with variable penetrance, not mandatory findings.
Source Section: PDF p. 21 | Double Stranded Repair > Fanconi Anemia
Notes: Features are characteristic associations consistent with MedlinePlus Genetics and GeneReviews (Fanconi Anemia). Marrow failure and AML risk overlap with other inherited bone-marrow-failure syndromes; pigmentary and skeletal findings are variable. Board-level overlap check advised.

Explanation: Bloom syndrome (BLM helicase deficiency) features pre/postnatal growth deficiency with short stature, a long narrow face, a sun-sensitive facial butterfly telangiectatic erythema appearing in infancy/early childhood, and a markedly increased risk of a wide range of early-onset cancers.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: BLM-related syndrome features; Congenital telangiectatic erythema features
Source Section: PDF p. 21 | Double Stranded Repair > Bloom Syndrome
Notes: Correction: 'Red skin rash' revised to the specific photosensitive facial butterfly telangiectatic erythema (hallmark of Bloom), and the cancer tile broadened to multiple early-onset cancers (MedlinePlus Bloom syndrome; Schnabel et al., Clin Genet 2021; Cunniff et al., Am J Med Genet A 2018; Nakano et al., Clin Cancer Res 2024). Precise rash wording resolves the prior HOLD. Board overlap: photosensitivity + cancer risk shared with xeroderma pigmentosum and other chromosomal-instability disorders - avoid co-placing them on one board. Elevated sister-chromatid exchange is the cytogenetic diagnostic hallmark.

Explanation: PCR amplification requires a DNA template, a pair of primers flanking the target, a thermostable DNA polymerase (Taq), and dNTP substrates (plus buffer and Mg2+). These are the core reagents.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Core PCR inputs; PCR amplification components
Source Section: PDF p. 28 | Polymerase Chain Reaction > Process
Notes: Core components verified (standard molecular biology). Buffer and Mg2+ are additional reagents not listed as tiles; no outlier.

Explanation: Each blot detects a specific macromolecule: Southern (DNA), Northern (RNA), Western (protein), Southwestern (DNA-binding proteins). Southwestern is distinct from Southern.
Source Section: PDF p. 30 | Southern, Western, Northern Blot
Notes: Method-target pairs verified (standard laboratory medicine). Caution: the paired-tile format reveals part of the association and may suit a learning mode over a competitive board.

Explanation: NF1 shows cafe-au-lait macules, iris Lisch nodules, cutaneous/plexiform neurofibromas, and an increased risk of pheochromocytoma (an associated complication, not present in all patients).
Source Section: PDF p. 38 | Genetics Concepts > Pleiotropy
Notes: Consistent with NF1 diagnostic criteria (NIH/standard references; MedlinePlus Genetics). Keep the type 1 qualifier; pheochromocytoma is an associated complication, not universal.

Explanation: Prader-Willi syndrome (loss of paternally expressed 15q11-q13) classically presents with neonatal hypotonia and poor feeding, followed in early childhood by hyperphagia, obesity, and hypogonadism. Features are age-dependent, not concurrent at birth.
Source Section: PDF p. 40 | Disorders of Imprinting > Prader-Willi Syndrome
Notes: Consistent with GeneReviews (Prader-Willi Syndrome) and MedlinePlus. Preserve age-dependent course: hypotonia is neonatal; hyperphagia/obesity emerge later.

Explanation: Angelman syndrome (loss of maternally expressed UBE3A) features a happy demeanor with frequent laughter, seizures, ataxic gait, and intellectual disability with severe speech impairment.
Source Section: PDF p. 40 | Disorders of Imprinting > Angelman Syndrome
Notes: Consistent with GeneReviews (Angelman Syndrome) and MedlinePlus. UBE3A imprinting is tissue-specific (brain); laughter is a characteristic behavior, not a diagnostic requirement.

Explanation: CF affects multiple digestive sites: pancreatic exocrine insufficiency (~80%) causing malabsorption and fat-soluble (A, D, E, K) vitamin deficiency, neonatal meconium ileus, and focal biliary cirrhosis/CF liver disease.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: GI and hepatobiliary manifestations of CF
Source Section: PDF p. 41 | Key Mutations > Cystic Fibrosis
Notes: Verified (Grasemann & Ratjen, NEJM 2023; CF Foundation hepatobiliary consensus, Sellers et al. 2024). Meconium ileus is neonatal; advanced/biliary cirrhosis affects only ~5-10%. Possible, not inevitable.

Connection Title: Respiratory and related findings in cystic fibrosis
Explanation: Defective CFTR-mediated airway surface hydration produces thick secretions, recurrent/chronic pulmonary infections, nasal polyps, and digital clubbing from chronic lung disease.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Pulmonary and upper airway CF findings
Source Section: PDF p. 41 | Key Mutations > Cystic Fibrosis
Notes: Consistent with Grasemann & Ratjen, NEJM 2023. Clubbing and recurrent infections are nonspecific (shared with other chronic suppurative lung diseases); the four-tile combination with nasal polyps improves specificity. Board overlap check advised.

Connection Title: Vaso-occlusive complications of sickle cell disease
Explanation: Vaso-occlusion drives dactylitis, acute chest syndrome, avascular necrosis (osteonecrosis), and ischemic stroke in sickle cell disease. Acute chest syndrome is multifactorial (infection, fat embolism, infarction), so this is an association with vaso-occlusion rather than an exclusive cause.
Source Section: PDF p. 41 | Key Mutations > Sickle Cell Anemia
Notes: Verified (Ware et al., Lancet 2017; Piel et al., NEJM 2017). Acute chest syndrome and stroke are not single-mechanism; keep association wording.

Connection Title: Additional classic sickle cell disease complications
Explanation: Sickle cell disease is associated with parvovirus B19-triggered transient aplastic crisis, functional autosplenectomy from repeated splenic infarction, Salmonella (and S. aureus) osteomyelitis, and renal papillary necrosis.
Source Section: PDF p. 41 | Key Mutations > Sickle Cell Anemia
Notes: Verified: Salmonella is a characteristic (not exclusive) cause of osteomyelitis in SCD, with S. aureus also common (Kao et al., Pediatr Blood Cancer 2020; NEJM Case 37-2023). Papillary necrosis and autosplenectomy confirmed (Ware et al., Lancet 2017). Associations, not universal findings.

Explanation: Duchenne muscular dystrophy (dystrophin deficiency, X-linked recessive) presents in early childhood (usually before age 5) with proximal weakness, Gowers sign, calf pseudohypertrophy, and a waddling gait. Early onset distinguishes it from later-onset Becker dystrophy.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Classic Duchenne findings; Childhood DMD presentation
Source Section: PDF p. 42 | Muscular Dystrophies > Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy
Notes: Consistent with GeneReviews (Dystrophinopathies) and MedlinePlus. First three features overlap with other myopathies; early onset (<5 y) improves specificity but onset varies. Keep the age qualifier.

Explanation: Beyond myotonia, myotonic dystrophy type 1 (CTG/DMPK) has multisystem features: posterior subcapsular cataracts, frontal balding, testicular atrophy/hypogonadism, and cardiac conduction defects/arrhythmias.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Systemic findings in DM1; Myotonic dystrophy type 1 clues
Source Section: PDF pp. 42-43 | Myotonic Dystrophy
Notes: Consistent with GeneReviews (Myotonic Dystrophy Type 1). Keep DM1 qualifier; balding and testicular atrophy apply to the appropriate sex/clinical context. Cardiac conduction disease is a key cause of mortality.

Explanation: Fragile X syndrome (FMR1 CGG expansion) features a long narrow face, prominent jaw/forehead, large protruding ears, and post-pubertal macroorchidism, alongside intellectual disability and autism-spectrum features.
Source Section: PDF p. 43 | Trinucleotide Repeat Expansion Diseases > Fragile X
Notes: Consistent with GeneReviews (FMR1 Disorders) and MedlinePlus. Macroorchidism is typically post-pubertal in affected males; expression varies with age and sex. Keep age/sex qualifier.

Explanation: Frataxin deficiency causes degeneration/hypoplasia of the dorsal root ganglia and dorsal (posterior) columns, spinocerebellar tracts, and lateral corticospinal tracts (with dentate nucleus involvement). The category spans both sensory ganglia and spinal tracts.
Source Section: PDF p. 43 | Friedreich Ataxia > Degeneration
Notes: Sites verified (Indelicato et al., Nat Rev Neurol 2025; Harding et al., Ann Neurol 2021; Santos et al., Antioxid Redox Signal 2010; Scott et al., CNS Drugs 2024). Dorsal root ganglia are sensory ganglia, not a spinal cord tract - do not retitle as 'four spinal cord tracts.'

Connection Title: Huntington disease psychiatric and motor presentation
Explanation: Huntington disease (CAG/HTT) combines psychiatric features (depression, irritability/aggression), early hyperkinetic chorea, and later hypokinetic/rigid parkinsonism. Motor features are stage-dependent.
Source Section: PDF p. 43 | Trinucleotide Repeat Expansion Diseases > Huntington Disease
Notes: Consistent with GeneReviews (Huntington Disease). Early chorea and late hypokinesia reflect different disease stages and need not coexist; psychiatric features vary. Keep stage qualifiers.

Explanation: Trisomy 13 (Patau) is associated with holoprosencephaly, cleft lip/palate, postaxial polydactyly, and cutis aplasia of the scalp, among other midline/CNS anomalies.
Source Section: PDF p. 44 | Autosomal Trisomies > Patau Syndrome
Notes: Characteristic associations consistent with standard genetics references (MedlinePlus; GeneReviews). Not all four required in every patient. Board overlap with trisomy 18 (GEN-029) advised.

Explanation: Trisomy 18 (Edwards) features a prominent occiput, micrognathia, clenched hands with overlapping fingers, rocker-bottom feet, and low-set ears. The combined pattern is characteristic.
Source Section: PDF p. 44 | Autosomal Trisomies > Edwards Syndrome
Notes: Consistent with standard genetics references (MedlinePlus; GeneReviews). Rocker-bottom feet and low-set ears are individually nonspecific (overlap with trisomy 13); the combination points to trisomy 18. Board overlap with Patau advised.

Explanation: Trisomy 21 is associated with duodenal atresia, Hirschsprung disease, atrioventricular septal defect (the characteristic cardiac lesion), and atlantoaxial instability. These are potential associated conditions, not universal.
Source Section: PDF p. 44 | Autosomal Trisomies > Down Syndrome
Notes: Verified (AAP Health Supervision for Down Syndrome, Bull et al. 2022; Kriss, Clin Pediatr 1999, PMID 10456238). Symptomatic atlantoaxial instability occurs in only ~1-2%; not universal.

Explanation: Trisomy 21 exam findings include a flat facial profile, single transverse palmar (simian) crease, epicanthal folds, and Brushfield spots of the iris, with variable expression.
Source Section: PDF p. 44 | Autosomal Trisomies > Down Syndrome
Notes: Consistent with AAP Down syndrome guideline (Bull et al. 2022). Individual features occur in unaffected individuals (e.g., single palmar crease in a minority of the general population); the combination is suggestive, not diagnostic.

Explanation: Cri-du-chat (5p deletion) features a high-pitched cat-like cry in infancy, microcephaly, low birth weight/growth failure, intellectual disability, and congenital heart disease such as VSD.
Source Section: PDF p. 45 | Microdeletion Syndromes > Cri-du-chat
Notes: Consistent with standard genetics references (MedlinePlus; GeneReviews, Cri-du-chat/5p deletion). VSD is an associated, not obligatory, finding; the characteristic cry changes/attenuates with age.

Connection Title: Williams syndrome cardiovascular and metabolic associations
Explanation: Williams syndrome (7q11.23 deletion including ELN) causes an elastin arteriopathy with supravalvular aortic stenosis and other arterial stenoses (e.g., renal artery), plus idiopathic hypercalcemia (~15-45%). The ELN deletion underlies the vascular phenotype; the other tiles are clinical associations.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Williams syndrome clues; Elastin-deletion syndrome associations
Source Section: PDF p. 45 | Microdeletion Syndromes > Williams Syndrome
Notes: Verified (Morris & Braddock, AAP Williams syndrome guideline 2020; Kozel et al., Nat Rev Dis Primers 2021; MedlinePlus). ELN deletion explains the arteriopathy (SVAS, renal/other arterial stenoses); hypercalcemia mechanism is distinct and not universal. Mixing a genetic lesion with clinical findings is intentional and medically coherent.
